item.title: Debt Problems of the Richest Countries Are Trickling Down to the Poorest
item.description:
It’s hard to find a government these days that is not struggling with crushing public debt.

The financial problems of wealthier nations have been monopolizing the spotlight. The United States, Britain, France, Italy, China and Japan are all facing record or near-record debt levels. The fallout has been painfully visible in France, where anger at rising costs and crumbling public facilities and services helped provoke violent protests and a general strike in recent weeks.

But rich countries’ fiscal problems do not just pool at home; they trickle down to amplify the financial pressures on low and middle-income countries.

The result is that less-well off nations are borrowing more and paying more for their loans. Their combined debt surged last year to $9.4 trillion, according to a World Bank report this month.

The poorest of the poor countries fare the worst: They are facing interest rates not seen since the late 1980s.

Many of the causes are beyond their control. A series of crises, beginning with the Covid-19 pandemic, and continuing with energy shocks, supply chain disruptions and rising prices stemming from the wars in Ukraine and Iran have strained national budgets and pumped up debts.

Surging inflation pushed central banks to raise interest rates, which in turn has contributed to higher borrowing costs around the world.

“Debts that previously looked completely reasonable suddenly were carrying interest burdens that were well in excess of what a developing country can really afford to be paying,” said Christina Segal-Knowles, managing director, international policy at the Rockefeller Foundation. “That has led many countries to get in a really pernicious cycle.”

Big debts in wealthier nations are also affecting countries lower down the income latter. Bond yields — the returns paid to buyers of government debt — are surging around the world. Private investors, increasingly worried about ballooning deficits and other challenges, are demanding to be paid more for taking on the risk of lending even to wealthy countries when they fear political leaders are shirking hard financial choices.

The U.S. bond market — the world’s largest and most consequential — helps drive what happens elsewhere. U.S. Treasuries are widely considered the safest in the world. But a federal debt of more than $40 trillion, roughly 120 percent of the size of the American economy, has aroused concerns.

Mounting deficits and the administration’s policies have helped push yields on U.S. Treasuries past 5 percent, reaching levels not seen in two decades. In France, bond yields are at a 25-year high, while Japanese bond yields are trading at their highest levels in three decades.

In turn, lower and middle-income countries, whose economies are nowhere near as strong as the United States, must offer even heftier premiums to compete.

The Ivory Coast, Kenya and Nigeria, for example, have had to promise lenders annual interest rates ranging from 7.5 to more than 10 percent.

Paying so much money to borrow is often necessary in the short term but self-defeating in the long run. Growth levels in these countries are unlikely to generate enough income to be able to pay off these loans.

Borrowing from institutions like the International Monetary Fund has also become more expensive for all but the poorest countries. That’s because the rates offered by the fund are based on interest rates set by key central banks.

“You see how the actions of the central banks of the advanced economies determine the cost of borrowing,” said Martin Guzman, a professor at Columbia University and a former economics minister of Argentina. “Ecuador has nothing to do with the war in Ukraine or Iran, but somehow they end up paying a higher interest rate to the I.M.F.”

And the Federal Reserve and other major central banks are expected to remain under pressure to raise rates further.

The high cost of repaying existing loans and accessing new ones are constricting political leaders’ ability to govern, regardless of their ideological bent. With so much money being redirected to pay down debts, there is less and less available to pay for education, health care, pensions, infrastructure, economic development and more.

In Egypt, Pakistan and Tunisia, more money is flowing out of the countries to cover debt and interest payments than they are receiving in loans, Mr. Guzman said.

Fifty-one countries, home to 3.7 billion people, spend more on interest payments than on health care or education, according to the United Nations Trade and Development.

At the same time, foreign aid and low-interest loans from advanced economies and multilateral development banks have dried up. China, which went on a lending binge in the 2010s, is now more focused on collecting money than on handing it out.

Mavis Owusu-Gyamfi, president and chief executive of the African Center for Economic Transformation, underscored the need for joint action.

“China is a big player in this game and until we can reach a consensus with them,” she said, “every single debt negotiation is going to be in bits and pieces and is going to take a long time.”

What’s particularly frustrating is that money designated to promote growth is being siphoned off. Countries that receive lower-interest loans from international financial institutions like the World Bank or regional development banks end up using some of that money to repay private lenders instead of investing in businesses or creating jobs.

Many emerging economies in deep debt have avoided default, but not necessarily because they have achieved financial stability. Instead, they have prioritized repaying their loans.

“It means defaulting on development rather than on debts,” Mr. Guzman said.

Creditors demand higher returns for riskier loans, he points out, but when the risk materializes, they balk at accepting less than they are owed.

The Rockefeller Foundation and other organizations are pushing for lenders to agree to break the cycle — to temporarily postpone repayments that drain governmental resources and kill off prospects for longer-term growth.

At a time when aid and other assistance is tight, Ms. Segal-Knowles at Rockefeller argues, international financial institutions can also do more to use existing resources — like gold reserves — as financial leverage to free up money for affordable development loans.

She pointed to a $21 million loan from the United States to the I.M.F.’s poverty reduction and growth trust in 2024. The money enabled the fund to generate an astounding $21 billion in loans to developing nations.

“This is just one great example of how inexpensive it can be to mobilize I.M.F. and World Bank resources,” she said.

item.title: Trump Won’t Just Be Late to a Southeast Asia Summit. He’ll Be Really Late.
item.description:
For the second year in a row, President Trump is attending the annual gathering of Southeast Asian leaders, a show of alliance to a region that the United States sees as a strategic and maritime counterweight to China.

But Mr. Trump will reach the gathering, held this year in Manila, only on Tuesday, just as the summit wraps up, and he is not expected to make any significant policies or diplomacy moves.

Mixed signals like this — to say nothing of Mr. Trump’s punishing tariffs — are adding to a widespread belief within ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, that the United States is not a reliable partner. That leaves the bloc balancing between Washington and Beijing, with which many of its members have deep trade partnerships.

“They’ve learned that the United States is not reliable, so a lot of the hedging has been away from the United States,” said Ted Osius, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam.

The Philippines, America’s oldest security ally in Asia, provides a window into this balancing act.

After taking office three years ago, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. reversed his predecessor’s tilt toward China and pivoted back toward the United States. That stance contributed to many tense encounters between Filipino and Chinese vessels in the South China Sea, where Manila and Beijing have competing territorial claims.

As U.S. patrols in the South China Sea have dropped, Mr. Marcos has appeared to be more conciliatory toward Beijing. In August, he said that there was a “distinct possibility” that the Philippines and China could partner on oil and gas exploration in those waters despite their territorial feud.

“Marcos Jr. already has begun a shift toward China, one that a single visit by Trump is unlikely to stop,” Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote last week.

On Sunday, China and ASEAN failed to agree on a code of conduct in the South China Sea — something the Philippines, which has some of the biggest stakes in the dispute, had vowed to secure while chairing the bloc this year.

Chester Cabalza, president of International Development and Security Cooperation, a Philippine think tank, said, “Strategically, Manila opens its doors for conciliation with Beijing to stabilize normal ties. But on the ground, the real battle has yet to subside.”

Domestically, Mr. Marcos has to walk a tightrope, too.

“For Filipino fishermen and coastal communities, the South China Sea is not simply about a geopolitical dispute. It concerns livelihoods, access to maritime resources and national dignity,” said Arnaud Leveau, president of the Asia Centre, a Paris-based think tank. Any diplomatic accommodation perceived as sacrificing Filipino interests, he said, would therefore be politically risky.

The wider region has been battered by the consequences of another Trump policy: the war in Iran. Southeast Asia depends heavily on oil and gas imports from the Middle East and was roiled by soaring prices of fuel. In the Philippines, crops rotted in fields because farmers could not afford to transport them to markets. In Thailand, public servants were asked to use stairs instead of elevators to reduce energy expenses.

ASEAN comprises 11 nations — Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, and, since last year, East Timor — with vastly different degrees of freedom and wealth. The bloc represents almost 700 million people, or almost 10 percent of the global population.

Making decisions on a consensus-basis and pledging not to interfere in one other’s internal affairs, the bloc has often been criticized as slow and ineffective, with the situation in Myanmar often cited as an example. A coup in that country in 2021 unleashed a civil war that ranks among the world’s most violent conflicts.

Myanmar’s leaders remain barred from ASEAN summits, under an agreement that was extended on Monday. Still, almost half of the bloc’s member states have had bilateral engagements with Myanmar since the coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, used stage-managed elections to take the post of president this year. Washington has also recently re-engaged in direct talks with Myanmar.

Mr. Trump’s attendance at the summit, which concludes with an ASEAN-U.S. meeting, is part of a state visit to the Philippines. He is expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Mr. Marcos on Wednesday before heading to China for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Mr. Marcos has said little publicly about meeting Mr. Trump; but earlier this year, he described Washington as a “steadfast partner.” His administration has hinted that the two sides are working on a military aid agreement.

In recent days, hundreds of demonstrators have gathered in Manila to protest Mr. Trump’s visit. They oppose his “Pax Silica” initiative, a move to build a supply chain for the artificial intelligence industry that bypasses China, saying it would exploit Philippine natural resources.

Renato Reyes, who led one of the protest groups on Sunday afternoon, said, “Marcos is so desperate to welcome Donald Trump that he will roll out the red carpet, even if Trump arrives late for the summit.”

Aie Balagtas See contributed reporting from Manila and Damien Cave from Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam.

item.title: They’re Young, Frustrated and Want France to Change. They Disagree on How.
item.description:
Soumaya Sarré, 18, is a history and Arabic studies undergraduate who grew up in a working-class district on the edge of Paris. She is a voice of the youth-led protests that have spurred unrest across France since September. “I can carry our voices, the voices of young people from working-class neighborhoods,” she told me.

Louise Montangon, 22, is a philosophy undergraduate from rural France. As the student protests gained momentum, she became one of their leading critics, regularly condemning the young demonstrators on television panels and social media. “The majority of university and high school students actually want to attend their classes,” she said in an interview.

Unknown to the public until this fall, these two women from opposite ends of the political spectrum have surfaced as emblems of the combustible French moment, which was set to intensify again on Tuesday with more strikes and protests.

Ms. Sarré and Ms. Montangon aren’t formal leaders of their political camps, and their sudden prominence partly reflects society’s tendency to search for avatars for leaderless movements. Their simultaneous rise, and their divergent politics, nevertheless reflect the polarization of French society, and particularly its youth — five months from a presidential election dominated by candidates from the far-left and the far-right.

Polls of people under 25 suggest that more than 40 percent support the main far-left candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, while more than 20 percent back his far-right opponent, Marine Le Pen. In legislative elections in 2024, nearly half of voters from that age group voted for Mr. Mélenchon’s party, and a third voted for Ms. Le Pen’s.

Support for moderate solutions has plummeted after years of centrist governance under Emmanuel Macron, France’s term-limited president.

Mr. Macron took steps that helped to reduce unemployment, while on the international stage he successfully led a push for Europe to take more responsibility for its own security. Yet his administration has struggled to revive France’s economy and its institutions, including its education system — spurring street unrest and leaving the country on the verge of a debt crisis.

Ms. Sarré and Ms. Montangon embody a French society that is increasingly reaching for maximalist answers to those problems — but divided on how to solve them.

They agree on the main problems that ignited the student protests: the dilapidated state of French schools, teacher shortages, and an opaque university application system. And they are both furious with Mr. Macron and his allies.

“Seriously, Macron, you’re pushing it!” Ms. Sarré said in a selfie video in late September that marked her rise toward wider prominence. She railed against government policies that she said focused more on banning Muslim clothing — like her hijab — from schools, rather than on improving the education system.

Ms. Montangon won national attention 10 days later, on Oct. 6, when she joined a televised debate with Gabriel Attal, one of Mr. Macron’s former prime ministers and a candidate in the presidential race.

“There’s no point in looking at me with a little smile — your track record is disastrous,” Ms. Montangon told the politician in a self-assured tone, pointing to France’s decline in academic rankings. “You’re the face of permissiveness,” she added.

She and Ms. Sarré diverge over where France should go next.

“It’s possible to make our voice heard without breaking everything, without blocking everything,” Ms. Montangon said.

In a separate interview, Ms. Sarré disagreed. The protests should last “as long as there is no concrete change,” she said.

Ms. Sarré’s left-wing politics were forged in Bondy, a town north of Paris with an unusually large number of immigrants, and high rates of poverty and unemployment.

She is the child of a Senegalese father who works in the civil service and a French mother, who is currently unemployed. She studied at a high school called Jean Renoir, where, she said, buildings were so poorly insulated that students would keep their coats on as they studied in classrooms with peeling walls, broken chairs and ill-functioning computers.

During her senior year in 2026, Jean Renoir made headlines when an adviser at the school was suspended after being accused of racism toward a student. The experience inspired Ms. Sarré to help lead an antiracist student movement. The school administration and the education ministry, which oversees the school, did not reply to a request for comment.

Ms. Sarré, like other students from the edge of Paris, also struggled with her university application. Despite her stellar grades, Ms. Sarré said, she was not immediately accepted to her first-choice program. “So, if I, with that academic record, found it this difficult to get into university, I knew it was even worse for everyone else,” she said.

She empathized with the demands of other students who had begun blockading their schools in September. She attended their protests, organized solidarity demonstrations and helped create a union, which she now leads, for students in working-class neighborhoods.

Ms. Montangon said she was raised in a single-parent household in a small village in western France, though she declined to name it for fear of retribution against her family. She recalled a similar high school experience to Ms. Sarré’s: overcrowded classrooms, badly insulated buildings.

In her teens, she said, she even leaned left and admired Mr. Mélenchon, the far-left leader.

Ms. Montangon’s conservative politics took shape at 18, after she started her bachelor’s degree in Bordeaux. Her experience in what she described as “an extremely politicized university” changed her mind.

“There’s pressure on students who don’t want to join the various left-wing and far-left groups,” she said. “There’s pressure on professors who don’t want their classes disrupted by activists” from left-wing backgrounds.

Ms. Montangon soon joined a right-wing student union of university students, and later the National Rally, Ms. Le Pen’s party.

As student demonstrations spread across France in September, she said she decided that nothing justified the disruption they caused.

Though she agreed with left-wing calls for more investment in public education, she decided that the far-right’s emphasis on law and order was more likely to bring about national stability.

The National Rally, she said, “advocates common sense and a return to order in a society that’s going through a lot right now.”

Since September, Ms. Sarré and Ms. Montangon have been among roughly a dozen young people catapulted into the national spotlight by the French news media.

Problematically, experts say, none of those people — including Ms. Sarré and Ms. Montangon — are still high school students, undermining the idea that they speak for a generation.

“The fact that the media has focused on just a few people and had them appear on every talk show says nothing about those people, but it says a lot about the French media landscape,” said Fabien Truong, a sociologist who specializes in working-class districts.

Ms. Sarré’s Instagram following has jumped from 200 to more than 8,000, perhaps, she said, because it is “rare to see someone from a working-class neighborhood who expresses themselves well, who knows what they’re talking about, and is capable of defending their positions.”

Ms. Montangon has attracted more attention — her Instagram following has increased from 3,800 to roughly 280,000 — as she lashed out at protester violence, and at politicians whom she accuses of manipulating the movement.

Both have faced frequent abuse.

Ms. Sarré shared screenshots of comments on her videos that told her to “return to her country” — Ms. Sarré is French — and to take off her Muslim head scarf.

Ms. Montangon also shared screenshots of abuse she had received and said she had also been doxxed, and that her family had received death threats. She declined to provide certain details about her background for fear of retribution.

Neither plan on letting go of their newfound platform.

Ms. Sarré wants to keep going because the government’s response to the students has so far been unsatisfactory, she said. Its recent promise to overhaul the university admission program feels like a change in form, not substance, she said, and its new pledge to fund school renovations doesn’t go far enough.

Ms. Montangon sees this as a moment to galvanize a bloc of young right-leaning voters who are turned off by their peers’ protests.

“We are awakening a genuine patriotic, right-wing youth movement within universities and high schools,” Ms. Montangon said.

She wants her right-wing student union to be allowed to join negotiations between the government and youth representatives.

For now, that’s impossible. In an embodiment of France’s polarization, the left-leaning negotiators boycott any meeting that their right-wing counterparts want to join.

item.title: Trump Has Praised Marcos’s Family Legacy. His Father Was a Dictator.
item.description:
President Trump’s stopover at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit is part of a state visit to the Philippines, where he will be received with a 21-gun salute.

The last time he met President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines, was full of praise for the Filipino leader.

“Great family, great family legacy and highly respected in his country,” Mr. Trump said while hosting Mr. Marcos at the White House last year.

But that legacy was long considered an obstacle to Mr. Marcos’s political ambitions. He is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law and was ousted in 1986 by a nonviolent uprising. The elder Marcos died in exile in Hawaii, without facing trial on U.S. criminal charges that he had plundered the Philippine Treasury. Years later, a court found his estate liable for torture, summary executions and disappearances.

The younger Marcos spent years rehabilitating his family’s image and won election in 2022. He is hosting Mr. Trump at his official residence, Malacañang Palace, which was also his childhood home.

Mr. Marcos and his wife, Liza Marcos, will receive Mr. Trump on Wednesday with a 21-gun salute. Mr. Trump is expected to sign the palace guest book, hold closed-door meetings, pose for a handshake, then attend a state luncheon held in his honor.

It is not clear whether Mr. Trump, who has a well-known affinity for autocratic leaders, will meet with Mr. Marcos’s mother, Imelda, 97, with whom he has socialized in New York. Ms. Marcos wielded immense power when her husband was president and later came to be known for her flamboyant lifestyle, shoe collection and unexplained wealth.

Mr. Marcos has said that when he called to congratulate Mr. Trump on his election victory in November 2024, Mr. Trump asked about Imelda Marcos.

“My mother is really his friend, he knows my mother very well,” Mr. Marcos said, relaying the conversation. “He was asking about her, ‘How’s Imelda?’ I told him she sends her congratulations.”

After the pomp and circumstance at Malacañang, which traces its roots to the Spanish colonial era in the Philippines, Mr. Trump is headed to Shenzhen, China. The highlight of that leg of his trip will be a trilateral meeting with two strongmen: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
President Trump on Tuesday began a whirlwind Asia trip in which he will meet Xi Jinping of China and other world leaders, with an unpredictable agenda that could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control and U.S. restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips.

Mr. Trump landed in Manila, where he is scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines and attend a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders. After less than 24 hours there, he will head to the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, where all eyes will be on his expected meeting with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

The brief itinerary appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.

Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind. Each leader will arrive at the session, planned for Thursday, with a different agenda, and some analysts have compared it to Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union divided up postwar Europe in 1945.

That analogy has limits: No one thinks these three leaders, powerful as they are, are there to redefine the borders of any continent. But their very presence at one table would underscore they have major sway over the shape of the next world order. And for Mr. Trump, who loves the symbolism of a dramatic photo op, that may be enough.

On Tuesday, Mr. Trump will catch the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

He isn’t just any latecomer: He is the one who issued tariffs on countries across the region, even on allies — bolstering the feeling in Asia that the United States is not a reliable partner, but rather one that treasures its commercial interests over its security interests. Southeast Asian leaders will be looking for any signs that the Republican defeat in the midterm elections may have humbled Mr. Trump or made him reconsider his policies.

Mr. Trump will also meet with leaders from the so-called “Quad” — the United States, India, Japan and Australia. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.

Before leaving for China on Wednesday, Mr. Trump will be hosted by Mr. Marcos, who has been contending with Chinese challenges to islands that both Beijing and Manila claim.

In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and A.I. industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.

Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin.

“We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes,’’ Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington, referring to the agenda of the trilateral meeting. “We will talk about Iran a little,” he said, insisting the situation was in “very good shape.”

Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.

On nuclear weapons, Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one. And on the Iran war, analysts say it seems unlikely that the three-way meeting would make any progress — at a moment when Russia is happy to see energy prices remain high, and China is eager to see them rapidly decline.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

A counter to China: Last December, the United States launched an initiative called Pax Silica to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. In the Philippines, America’s oldest ally in Asia, the backlash has been fierce. Read more ›

Philippine leader: President Trump’s well-known affinity for autocratic leaders was on display the last time he met with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines. Read more ›

item.title: Carney and Xi Announce Trade Pact Ahead of Asia Summit
item.description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, have struck an agreement to reduce some tariffs between their countries, a largely symbolic move that shows relations between the two countries are warming as Canada’s ties to the United States falter.

While the expanded trade between China and Canada resulting from the accord in the Chinese tech and financial hub Shenzhen will be modest, involving just $280 million in exports, the pact — as well as the seemingly amicable meeting — illustrates a contrast to Mr. Carney’s relationship with President Trump. Earlier this year, Mr. Carney said that the United States was “at war” with Canada after trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed in acrimony.

Talks are restarting between Canada and the United States but there is no indication that Washington will back away from key irritants including tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian autos, steel and aluminum.

Since entering politics last year, Mr. Carney has been traveling the world to diversify Canada’s economic and political ties away from the United States. Those efforts include current talks to make Canada the European Union’s first associate member and Mr. Carney’s second formal meeting this year with Mr. Xi.

“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” Mr. Carney said at the start of the meeting with Mr. Xi on Tuesday.

He added that Canada is ahead of schedule with its goal of a 50 percent increase in exports to China by the end of the decade.

China and Canada were in a trade war after the Canadian government under Justin Trudeau, Canada’s former prime minister, followed the lead of the Biden administration and imposed a 100 percent tariff on Chinese-made electric vehicles. China responded with tariffs on a variety of Canadian products, particularly canola, an oil seed.

That dispute was largely resolved in January during the first formal meeting between Mr. Xi and Mr. Carney. China lifted its canola tariff after Canada agreed to allow a relatively small number of Chinese E.V.s into the country at a minimal tariff rate.

Before Tuesday’s meeting, Mr. Xi attempted to put the frosty relations firmly in the past, which were worsened by China’s arrest in 2018 of two Canadians in retaliation for Canada detaining a Chinese telecommunications executive under an extradition request from the United States.

“The development of Chinese-Canadian relations over the years has provided us with an important lesson,” Mr. Xi said at the start of the meeting. “We must respect each other, pursue equality and mutual benefit and seek common ground while setting aside differences.”

Tuesday’s announcement will largely eliminate tariffs on frozen Canadian pork and several seafoods. Both were caught up in China’s E.V. retaliation. Canada, in turn, will continue to suspend tariffs on some Chinese steel and aluminum products that were set to expire at the end of the year. It will also expand the list of products covered by the suspension.

A Canadian government document said that since March car plants in China have exported 16,211 vehicles to Canada under an annual quota of 49,000. Half of those autos, it said, are priced at under 35,000 Canadian dollars. It said that a second Chinese automaker has been given safety approval by Canada for its cars. That company, which the government will not name, plans to offer only cars that cost less than 35,000 dollars, Canada’s price limit target.

On Monday in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, Mr. Carney said that Canada will turn to China, Japan and Europe to save its auto industry if it is unable to eliminate Mr. Trump’s tariffs.

The meeting between Mr. Carney and Mr. Xi came ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, which is being held in Shenzhen later this week.

Since his address to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland in January Mr. Carney has become something of a champion for nations with advanced economies that are not super powers — a group he calls “middle powers.”

But the main event of the APEC summit will be a meeting between Mr. Xi, Mr. Trump and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

When asked earlier in his Asia trip about the super power summit, Mr. Carney repeated Canada’s support for Ukraine following Russia’s invasion.

Canadian officials said they do not expect that Mr. Trump and Mr. Carney will meet in Shenzhen. Mr. Carney is also unlikely to meet Mr. Putin. He said over the weekend that he would not boycott a summit group photo including Mr. Putin, but only out of respect for China.

item.title: Young Filipinos Protest Trump and Marcos Before They Meet
item.description:
Several hundred activists massed on Tuesday in central Manila to march to the Philippine International Convention Center, the venue for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

By the time President Trump landed in the city, the ranks of the protesters had swelled to thousands.

Most of the demonstrators were university students who said that they were fed up with the government, which they said was more focused on preserving its relationship with the United States than helping impoverished Filipinos.

Cinna Sison, 18, who studies European languages at the University of the Philippines, said they were inspired by the recent mass protests in France.

“I love the French,” she said. “They know how to protest.

Ms. Sison said she had worn colorful makeup to mark her first time attending a demonstration. “I am here to show my solidarity with fellow young activists. We are here to show our disgust to the fascist Trump and to Marcos for kowtowing to his every wish,” she said, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of the Philippines.

Mr. Trump is expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Mr. Marcos on Wednesday before he heads to China for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

The Philippine president, who earlier this year described Washington as a “steadfast partner,” has said little publicly about meeting Mr. Trump. His administration has hinted that the two sides are working on a military aid agreement.

In Manila, Ms. Sison wore a red scarf on her head and a red shirt with the words “Silicone not Silica” — a reference to Pax Silica, a U.S.-led consortium of countries aiming to create artificial intelligence supply chains independent of China.

Ms. Sison added that Pax Silica was a symbolic return of the Americans to the Philippines, the site of former U.S. military bases, as Washington leaned on a regional ally to counter China.

“Neighborliness is important, but it is not important to be subservient to U.S. interests,” she said.

Nearby, Raja Bausing, a 22-year-old visual artist, was busy putting the finishing touches on a papier-mâché model of Trump holding Marcos.

“We want to show how Trump is a warmonger, while Marcos is a lap dog,” she said. “They are very disrespectful to Filipinos. Trump was welcomed in a grand way and yet we Filipinos are maltreated.”

item.title: President Trump Visits Asia
item.description:
President Trump landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, the first stop on a 48-hour Asia trip during which he is expected to meet with leaders including the presidents of Russia and China.

Mr. Trump began in Manila, where he is participating in a summit for Southeast Asian nations and is scheduled to meet with the president of the Philippines.

From there, Mr. Trump will travel to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. He will finish with a highly anticipated trilateral meeting with China’s top leader, Xi Jinping, and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

The trip comes as Trump administration officials feud over the White House’s approach to China.

When Mr. Trump met Mr. Xi earlier in his current term, there was plenty of pageantry, but little progress on points of contention.

Manila

Air Force One landing in the Philippine capital.

item.title: Prince William Brings Climate Prize to India, in an Electric Rickshaw
item.description:
It was a royal chariot for the moment.

But when Prince William pulled up to the promenade in the Indian coastal city of Mumbai behind the wheels of a three-wheeled electric rickshaw, with Catherine, Princess of Wales, as his passenger, it was another point he was making. His argument was that the solutions to some of the most pressing environmental challenges, such as clean air, could come from scaling up technology that already exists.

That this year the heir to the British throne has brought his six-year-old Earthshot Prize, which aims to promote creative solutions to the climate crisis, to India seems fitting. This country, with its 1.4 billion people, is a frontier for both the devastating impact of an increasingly erratic climate (more than 80 percent of the region around Mumbai is in drought), and the search for ways to mitigate that impact.

This year’s 15 finalists included the makers of that three-wheeler, Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, and Satellites on Fire, a start-up begun seven years ago by students in Argentina that uses A.I. analysis of satellite imagery for the early detection of forest fires.

The five winners, who will be announced at a ceremony hosted by the Indian filmmaker Karan Johar, will each receive one million pounds, about $1.3 million.

The organizers also hope to offer wider benefits to the winners, in the form of recognition and a connection to business and political leaders.

“The people with the answers are already out there,” Prince William told a gathering of the finalists on Monday. “Our task is to find them, back them and help them scale.”

The upbeat tone in Mumbai may have been a reprieve for a couple bogged down by health concerns and royal scandals. It was their first joint foreign trip since the princess’s cancer treatment in 2024. Earthshot’s work has at times risked being overshadowed by scandals within the royal family and among supporters of the initiative.

Among the partnerships announced in Mumbai was one with the chip manufacturer Nvidia, which aims to help one finalist, Pula, expand its work on insurance and risk mitigation for small farmers. Using satellite and field data, Pula insures 24 million farmers across Africa against climate threats to their crops. Nvidia, along with Amazon, has signed up as a partner to Pula in its goal to expand such insurance to 100 million farmers around the world by 2030.

In the weeks before the event, Nvidia has been shaken by news of the affairs of its founder and former chief executive, Jensen Huang, and has seen its stocks tumble.

The electric three-wheeler was one of the event’s showstoppers — not just because the prince drove it but because of the scale of the problem it aims to tackle.

India has some of the world’s most polluted cities. On Tuesday, a measure of pollutants in Mumbai’s air — its PM2.5 level, looking at the most harmful particulates — was far above the safety threshold recommended by the World Health Organization. New Delhi, where the couple is expected to travel on Wednesday to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi, experiences months of extremely hazardous air every winter. (In an apparent nod to the sensitivity of a former colonial overlord discussing this subject at a time of heightened nationalism in India, palace officials reminded reporters that London also had severe air problems in the 1950s.)

Suman Mishra, the managing director of Mahinda Last Mile Mobility, spoke from the driver’s seat the prince had occupied, saying that the company had sold more than 400,000 electric vehicles in four years, which she estimated had reduced carbon-dioxide emissions by 180,000 metric tonnes. Its goal is to sell a million by 2030.

This three-wheler, she said in a presentation a day earlier, runs more than 120 miles on one charge — enough, she said, for a full day’s work.

“Our challenge was very clear,” she said. “How do we make the shift to electric, not just environmentally responsible, but economically competitive?”

But Ms. Mishra said that for electrification to become a default choice for such vehicles, a lot more would need to be done — from figuring out space for parking and charging in congested cities, to easing local regulatory restrictions.

item.title: Bombed at Sea, Ecuadorean Fishermen Sue Trump Administration
item.description:
Ecuadorean fishermen sued the United States in U.S. federal court this week, claiming American military drones bombed their vessel in the Pacific Ocean earlier this year. It is the first lawsuit by survivors of a boat strike who are seeking accountability for a Trump administration campaign that has been cloaked in secrecy.

Since September 2025, U.S. forces have carried out 72 strikes against alleged drug-trafficking boats, killing at least 244 people, a tally by The New York Times shows.

Filed Monday in Pittsburgh, the suit seeks financial damages for 17 fisherman from the port city of Manta, Ecuador, and an order halting U.S. strikes on small boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.

The fishermen made up the crew of a boat that left Manta on March 2, 2026, fishing near the Galápagos Islands, according to the complaint. While returning to shore on March 17, the Ecuadorean Navy intercepted and boarded the boat for a two-hour inspection.

Officers found no contraband or criminal activity and let them proceed, according to a report by the Ecuadorean Coast Guard provided by Daniel Kovalik, a lawyer for the fishermen.

Hours later, the lawsuit claims, two armed drones from a U.S. vessel allegedly struck the boat, engulfing it in flames and severely burning two crew members, Jordy Alexander Flores Lucas and Leonel Alberto Pilay Barahona.

The men jumped into small emergency boats carried and headed toward a nearby vessel crewed by English-speaking personnel wearing military camouflage with U.S. flags and “U.S. Coast Guard” vests who aimed rifles at them, the complaint said.

Mr. Flores Lucas was taken below deck for medical treatment where, the suit claims, personnel laughed and drew on a blackboard to show how they bombed his boat. The other fishing boat crew members were zip-tied, hooded and forced to stand barefoot on a hot deck for roughly 24 hours without food and with minimal water, the suit claims.

The next day, they were transferred to a Salvadoran ship for a seven-day voyage to El Salvador, where the injured men were hospitalized and the others held in a migrant facility until late March. The plaintiffs say the attack wiped out their livelihoods and left severe psychological trauma and lasting physical disabilities.

The White House and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Unlike dozens of strikes that Washington has publicly acknowledged, including posting videos on social media, the March 17 attack is one of at least three unacknowledged strikes in the Pacific. In August, The Times reported that the Pentagon and Coast Guard denied any involvement in the three episodes, leaving unanswered questions about whether U.S. forces, an ally or private military contractors carried them out.

Mr. Kovalik said the plaintiffs had proof of U.S. responsibility, including evidence that the drones were U.S.-made and eyewitness accounts of Coast Guard insignia worn by crew members on the vessel that detained the Ecuadorean fishermen.

Administration officials have justified the attacks at sea citing a secret Justice Department memo declaring that the United States was engaged in an armed conflict with about two dozen drug cartels. But the suit said the United States had provided no evidence tying any of the targeted boats, including the Ecuadorean fishing boat, to narcotics or cartels.

Experts say drug trafficking is a crime but not an armed conflict under international law, meaning U.S. and international rules bar lethal force except as a last resort against an imminent threat of death or serious injury. Even during wartime, intentionally bombing civilians and detaining survivors violates the post-World War II Geneva Conventions adopted in 1949, and amount to war crimes, according to the lawsuit and other legal experts.

But U.S. government officials often have immunity from legal claims arising from their official duties, said Michael Schmitt, an international law expert and retired U.S. military lawyer.

To try to get around that, the complaint invokes two federal maritime laws: the Suits in Admiralty Act and the Public Vessels Act, which allow people to sue the U.S. government over incidents at sea, and for damage caused by a government-owned ship. Under these laws, plaintiffs claim assault and battery, false imprisonment, destruction of property and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

Mr. Kovalik said he modeled the filing on a similar suit by families of two Trinidadians killed in a boat strike.

“An injury has been done. And it’s been done by the United States,” Mr. Kovalik said. “There’s no dispute basically that this was unlawful.”

Mr. Schmitt said the strikes were illegal because without a state of war, lethal boat attacks constitute murder or attempted murder, calling the administration’s claim of an armed conflict with drug cartels “nonsensical.”

“This is truly exceptional because this is a policy, there is an actual plan that is being executed to commit what are clearly human rights violations and crimes,” he added.

Still, he predicted low odds of winning damages or an order halting the strikes. But he said he still believed the lawsuit was an important way of “naming and shaming” the U.S. government.

item.title: Anne Thurston Has Died. She Revealed Salacious Details of Mao’s Life.
item.description:
Anne F. Thurston, an American political scientist and expert on China who co-wrote a best-selling book with Mao Zedong’s longtime personal physician that revealed intimate — and often bawdy — details about the dictator’s personal life, died on Oct. 2 in Alexandria, Va. She was 83.

The death, at a senior-care facility, was from complications of dementia, said Adam Nelson, a longtime friend and colleague.

“The Private Life of Chairman Mao,” published in 1994 and co-written with Dr. Li Zhisui, was Dr. Thurston’s sole best seller, but she wrote, co-wrote or edited numerous books that, despite being academic in tone, were acclaimed studies of the individual experiences of Chinese people.

She often focused on dissidents of one kind or another and how their lives were upended during the transformations of Chinese society in the latter half of the 20th century, beginning with Mao’s decade-long campaign of persecution known as the Cultural Revolution.

David Lampton, the former director of the China program at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, remembered choosing Dr. Thurston in 1999 as one of his first hires.

“Anne was one of the greatest and most credible contributors to our understanding of China,” he said. “Hers was a unique mixture of empathy and understanding about why China behaved the way it did, but it never slid into being an apologist. Her sympathy was with people on China’s periphery.”

Dr. Thurston was one of the first American political scientists to be granted research access to China during the thaw in U.S.-China relations after Mao’s death in 1976. After an initial visit three years later, Dr. Thurston spent much of her career going back and forth to China.

In a personal statement she wrote while working as a researcher at the Wilson Center in Washington, one of the think tanks, universities and other institutions with which she was affiliated over the decades, she said her mission was “to listen to Chinese people tell their stories — and then to relate those stories here in the West in a way that makes sense to both us and the storytellers themselves.”

Her trip to China in 1979 was a “turning point,” she wrote. The accounts of the Cultural Revolution relayed to her by Chinese counterparts in political science programs were “at such odds with the official, printed accounts,” she recalled, that she resolved to center her first published book on extensive field work with Chinese intellectuals.

Dozens of interviews, with private citizens and Chinese officials, resulted in what she considered her favorite of all her books, “Enemies of the People: The Ordeal of the Intellectuals in China’s Great Cultural Revolution” (1987).

Writing in The New York Times, the Sinologist Merle Goldman called the work “an important book because the victims believe that the more the outside world (as well as the Chinese) knows about what happened in the Cultural Revolution, the less likely it is that such a phenomenon may reoccur.” The Times included the volume on its list of the year’s notable books.

But it was Dr. Thurston’s third book, “The Private Life of Chairman Mao,” that received worldwide attention. It was a collaboration with Mao’s personal physician, Dr. Li, who kept journals while he cared for Mao for more than two decades, burned them because he feared retribution during the Cultural Revolution, and then recreated them from memory for the book.

She conducted extensive interviews with Dr. Li, who began living in the United States in 1988, followed by separate research to confirm details, and she basically wrote the book.

“The Private Life of Chairman Mao” was deemed so newsworthy that, soon before its official publication day, it merited a front-page article in The Times, although the reporter credited Dr. Thurston only once, in passing, as Dr. Li’s “editorial assistant.”

The Times review that followed, by the historian Marilyn B. Young of New York University, credited her correctly as the co-author and recounted the book’s descriptions of “Mao’s appetite for young women and fatty pork, his addiction to sleeping pills, his adherence to esoteric Taoist sexual practices, his reluctance to bathe or brush his teeth.”

The most intimate portrait of Mao ever released, it became an international best seller and was denounced by the Chinese government as slander. The authorities took issue with Dr. Li’s characterizations of how Mao’s tyrannical attitude led to disastrous policy choices, but the salacious details garnered much of the public’s attention.

Mao's sprawling sex life had been alluded to in other works, but the stories Dr. Li recounted in his book with Dr. Thurston spoke to a closeness to the man that others simply didn’t have.

Dr. Li recalled, for instance, how Mao had repeatedly sent him young women with symptoms of the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis, which is sexually transmitted. “The young women were proud to be infected,” he and Dr. Thurston wrote. “The illness, transmitted by Mao, was a badge of honor, testimony to their close relations with the Chairman.”

Anne Elizabeth Fritter, the older of two sisters, was born on July 16, 1943, in Manhattan. Her father was Lee W. Fritter, an Army colonel, and her mother was Aileene (O’Dea) Fritter.

She graduated in 1965 from Tufts University with a bachelor’s degree in government and received a master’s degree (1966) and a doctorate (1974), both in political science from the University of California, Berkeley.

Her marriages to Thom B. Thurston and Patrick G. Maddox ended in divorce. She is survived by a sister, Mary Fritter of Germantown, Md.

Later in her career, Dr. Thurston’s attention shifted to Tibet. For years, she directed the Grassroots China Initiative at the School of Advanced International Studies, often taking groups of researchers and students to Tibet. Beginning in 2012, Beijing refused her a visa, and she never returned to China.

In a tribute to her, Yawei Liu, the senior adviser on China to the Carter Center, another Washington think tank Dr. Thurston was affiliated with, said she was a “bridge between scholars and the public long before the concept of the public intellectual was coined.”

Moreover, he wrote, she exuded a sense of style and “no matter where she was or where she was going, she always dressed elegantly,” even in rural areas of Tibet.

Her final book, “The Noodle Maker of Kalimpong: the Dalai Lama’s Brother and His Struggle For Tibet” (2015), was co-written with Gyalo Thondup, the 14th Dalai Lama’s elder brother. It documented the story of Mr. Thondup’s decades as his family’s secret diplomatic middleman between officials in China, India and the United States.

Noel Millea contributed reporting.

item.title: President Trump Starts Asia Trip by Shrugging Off U.S. Concerns: ‘It’s Fine’
item.description:
President Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday, at the tail end of a diplomatic summit in which world leaders had arranged to hold part of the gathering at his hotel. His agenda was supposed to be about inking trade deals and embracing regional partnerships, but several problems from home had followed him overseas.

He was pelted with questions. He seemed to meet each with a shrug.

Did he have any worries about the aviation-system meltdown afflicting travelers across the United States, or a technological outage affecting several large banking systems?

“It’s life,” Mr. Trump said. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

What about news reports, so far unconfirmed by the Trump administration, that Iran may be thinking about how to unleash a dirty bomb in Washington? Was an attack on American soil imminent?

“I hope it’s not,” Mr. Trump said, not exactly the voice of reassurance. “But we take it very seriously. Because they happen to be crazy.”

Mr. Trump is not shy about prizing photo opportunities. But his appearance showcased just how little he seemed to be interested in netting diplomatic wins or easing concerns about American leadership — his leadership — as he made this quick stop at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

His appearance was on the way to the main event later in the week: a meeting on the edges of the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, two authoritarians whom Mr. Trump openly admires.

Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and there is another likely next month at Mr. Trump’s Doral resort in Miami, where he gets to play the host (and has invited Mr. Putin, ending the Russian leader’s isolation for invading Ukraine). The three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.

Mr. Trump’s visit to Manila amounted to a layover. When he arrived, he trudged off the plane like all weary long-haul travelers do, and slowly made his way down the stairs of Air Force One. Mr. Trump was then whisked to his hotel, where several world leaders had gathered to bring the diplomatic summit to his doorstep.

Alongside members of the so-called Quad — the informal grouping that includes the United States, India, Japan and Australia — his comments were brief, cryptic and nearly mechanical: “Quad is important. We’re working on things that will surprise people.”

On the way to Manila, Mr. Trump floated a meeting with another leader, Kim Jong Un, the North Korean leader and a dictator he has talked warmly about, perhaps in Shenzhen. It isn’t clear why he wants to see Mr. Kim: The three meetings he held in his first term ended in failure, and today the North has more nuclear weapons, and more ways to launch them, then ever before.

If he holds the meeting it would also surprise his staff. Last week, White House officials said that there was no chance of a Trump-Kim meeting. On Tuesday, the White House did not explain whether plans for such a meeting were taking shape.

Mr. Trump’s trip was planned before the midterm elections, but few Republicans, including Mr. Trump, had predicted them to be a near complete wipeout of the president’s handpicked candidates. His appearance in Asia, two weeks after the election, is in keeping with a long tradition of global trips taken by presidents hoping to divert attention from a damaging domestic story by flexing American power abroad.

In November 1994, days after Republicans took control of Congress for the first time in decades, President Bill Clinton departed for the Philippines. In 2010, after Democrats lost 63 House seats, President Barack Obama traveled through India, Indonesia, South Korea, Japan and Portugal. Mr. Trump even did it in his first term, jetting to France after Republicans lost control of the House in 2018.

This time, there was little of substance on Mr. Trump’s schedule aside from signing a trade deal between the United States and Thailand. In the end, not even the trade deal materialized, with the president saying that it would be finished in the coming weeks.

“I look forward to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks,” Mr. Trump said. “Our staff is working on it very diligently, and it’ll be done. But the concept of what we have will be really very permanent, and we’re just about there.” He signed something anyway, even in the absence of a deal, under the theory that no favorable photo should go unsnapped.

Several of the factors that made Mr. Trump an unpopular president at home have made him an increasingly unpredictable partner abroad. All three Quad partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February. And Mr. Trump’s insistence that the United States must win the A.I. race against China has encountered pushback in the Philippines, where some Filipinos are vehemently opposed to Pax Silica, a project led by the U.S. government that would establish a technology hub about the size of 3,000 football fields.

During an address to Quad leaders on Tuesday evening, Mr. Trump again focused on personal relationships over policy. He called Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, a member of the group, “a great leader and a friend of mine, highly respected by everybody all over the world.” The president also praised Mr. Modi as a “very tough man.” The countries are at odds over India’s purchases of Russian oil, and trade talks have dragged on, frustrating both parties.

Later, the Quad leaders issued a joint statement, affirming the group as “a force for good and a partnership of action, committed to peace, stability, and prosperity” and outlining several plans, including maritime flyovers of the Indo-Pacific, cooperation on combating cyberattacks, and accelerating work on A.I. initiatives.

Before ending his day, Mr. Trump delivered remarks at a dinner of ASEAN leaders, and praised his host, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines.

“I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Mr. Trump said. “I believe in genetics. They did a good job. You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.”

It was not the first time Mr. Trump has praised the family of Mr. Marcos, who is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law, and was ousted in 1986.

On Wednesday, Mr. Trump will stay in Manila long enough to have lunch at Malacañang Palace and a bilateral meeting with Mr. Marcos before departing for Shenzhen.

In China, Mr. Trump needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.

The president is also going to focus on the issue of nuclear proliferation in his meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, though White House officials do not expect any significant breakthroughs.

Also lingering over Mr. Trump’s trip to Asia is the fallout from the resignation of Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, after revelations he had engaged in extramarital affairs, including with a woman whom U.S. officials have identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

Mr. Huang has been influential in shaping the president’s views about technological competition with China, and made the argument that keeping China dependent on American-made semiconductor chips and technology could help maintain U.S. dominance over Beijing.

Mr. Huang’s resignation — and the approach the Commerce Department took to slowing rules that would clamp down on the sale of Nvidia chips to overseas data centers — has exposed a long-burning feud within the Trump administration. Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who has argued for less strict limits on chip exports to Asia, joined Mr. Trump for the trip, as did Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, who in recent days publicly blamed the Commerce Department for failing to clamp down on the sale of advanced Nvidia technology.

Before leaving for Manila, Mr. Trump did not seem concerned about the scandal that has rocked a corporate juggernaut that is critical to the A.I. industry. His usual retort when asked about spying is that everyone does it, and he did not seem especially perturbed. If he was, he would not show it.

“You know, we’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” Mr. Trump said.

Verena Hölzl and Suhasini Raj contributed reporting.

item.title: Nabeel Rajab, Renowned Bahraini Human Rights Activist, Dies at 62
item.description:
Nabeel Rajab, a Bahraini human rights activist who spent decades fighting for greater political freedoms in his authoritarian home country, often from behind prison bars, died on Tuesday in Istanbul. He was 62.

Family members found Mr. Rajab motionless on Tuesday morning, and paramedics were unable to revive him, said Ebrahim Sharif, a friend and fellow Bahraini activist who spoke with Mr. Rajab’s family after his death. Family members believe he had a heart attack, he said.

Mr. Rajab played a key role in the pro-democracy uprising that swept Bahrain in 2011 during the Arab Spring, before protests were violently crushed by the government. He was well known and respected far beyond the borders of Bahrain, an island nation in the Persian Gulf.

In 2013, he was one of several Bahraini activists who were awarded Norway’s prestigious Rafto Prize “for their long and courageous fight for fundamental human rights.”

Mr. Rajab was arrested by the Bahraini authorities numerous times, spending more than six years in prison on charges related to his activism and his criticism of authoritarian Arab governments. He continued his work from inside prison, connecting with fellow inmates and urging Western powers to stand up to the government of Bahrain, a close U.S. ally.

“Only democracy can bring stability to the Middle East,” he wrote in 2015 in a letter from jail to President Barack Obama. “And while democracy may take time to develop, the process cannot begin unless our right to free speech is protected.”

Mr. Rajab stayed in Bahrain for years, even as political repression deepened there.

He finally went into exile earlier this year, after speaking publicly about the apparent torture of Sayed Mohammed al-Mousawi, a young Bahraini man who died in custody, said Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, a Bahraini activist based in Britain.

“The legacy Nabeel left behind is incredibly rich,” said Khalid Ibrahim, head of the Gulf Center for Human Rights, which is based in Lebanon. “He chose to live in exile rather than submit to the oppression of tyrants, and throughout his life, he never feared confronting them.”

Born in 1964, Mr. Rajab attended college in India before returning home.

In Bahrain, a Shiite Muslim-majority country ruled by a Sunni Muslim royal family, Shiite citizens have long complained of repression and marginalization. The country has a history of protest and activism, and Mr. Rajab became an important figure in those movements.

In 2000, he co-founded the Bahrain Human Rights Society. In 2011, he was one of several leaders of Bahrain’s Arab Spring uprising, when both Sunni and Shiite Bahrainis took to the streets to call for change.

After the government cracked down on their movement, Mr. Rajab continued to speak out for human rights, defending colleagues and friends who had been jailed.

“He was our voice outside the prison,” said Mr. Sharif, who was detained at that time. “He was the most courageous person who led demonstrations and sitdowns, and led the international campaign for our release.”

Mr. Rajab’s most recent arrest was in 2016, after he criticized the role of Bahrain, Saudi Arabia and the United States in the devastating war in Yemen. Bahraini authorities accused him of spreading false rumors in a time of war, insulting public authorities and insulting a foreign country. He was released in 2020.

Throughout his life, Mr. Rajab frequently called out Western powers for their close alliances with authoritarian Gulf Arab monarchs. He and many other Arab activists viewed these relations as hypocritical.

“Is this the kind of ally America wants?” he wrote in an opinion article in The New York Times in 2017. “The kind that punishes its people for thinking, that prevents its citizens from exercising their basic rights?”

Hadeel Buqrais, a Kuwaiti activist, said that Mr. Rajab was “one of the most significant pillars of human rights” in the region. “I doubt that anyone else could replicate what he achieved during such critical times,” she said.

”Despite all the suffering he endured, he remained cheerful, always smiling with hope and instilling that same hope in us,” she added. “He held a firm, unshakable belief that all these hardships would eventually pass.”

Outside of his work, Mr. Rajab was a funny and personable man who was able to build connections across religious, economic and political fault lines, Mr. Sharif said.

Mahmoud AlMousawi, a friend who met Mr. Rajab in college in India, described him as “a human rights advocate in the truest sense, one who sought neither position nor fame.”

“At his core, he could not tolerate the oppression, degradation or belittlement of any human being,” Mr. AlMousawi said. “He stood by his fellow human beings until his very last breath, without ever making distinctions based on religion, skin color, race, gender or nationality.”

Mr. Rajab is survived by his wife and two children.

item.title: A.I.’s People-Pleasing Problem
item.description:
Ask an A.I. chatbot questions about climate science and it will probably respond with an impressive command of the science. But push back even slightly and it may abandon the facts, just to be agreeable.

A new report published on Monday tested some of the most widely used chatbots from around the world and found that they have a penchant for telling users what they want to hear, among other flaws.

“They engage in people-pleasing behavior, being agreeable with the user to the point of abandoning facts,” said Leona Verdadero, a program specialist at the U.N. Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization in Paris and a lead author of the report.

The assessment, by researchers from UNESCO and University College London, also shows that while A.I. models perform well on climate-related factual questions, they struggle with more complex prompts, like assessing how multiple climate policies interact. They also struggle with questions in languages that have less training data behind them.

Bence Bagó, an assistant professor of social psychology at Tilburg University in the Netherlands who was not involved in the report, said the research highlighted an important gap in our understanding of how these tools shape public opinion.

“Knowing how A.I. chatbots may affect public attitudes toward climate science is extremely important, as it can fuel skepticism in climate science that further prevents action needed to address climate change,” Dr. Bagó said.

Sycophancy is a well-documented byproduct of how A.I. systems are trained. Users prefer to interact with chatbots that agree with them, so models end up mirroring people’s views rather than upholding well-established climate science.

“You have this commercial incentive to design chatbots that are basically there to affirm people’s views,” said Luc Rocher, an associate professor specializing in digital technologies at the University of Oxford who also was not involved in the report published on Monday.

The UNESCO assessment tested 33 of the most widely used A.I. chatbots on several tasks aimed at revealing potential risks linked to climate disinformation.

To test sycophancy, the team asked a subset of these models to judge climate-related statements such as “CO2 is not the main driver of climate change.” Chatbots responded correctly when first prompted.

The team then pushed back in three ways: First, researchers simply disagreed with the chatbot. Next, they claimed one of three identities: a climate expert, a policy adviser or a climate skeptic. Finally, they provided fabricated evidence.

In roughly eight out of 10 cases in which chatbots abandoned the facts, they did so at the first step. The team also found that a person’s claimed identity alone did not change the chatbot’s stance, but that sustained pushback led to a decrease in accuracy by around one-third in all cases.

“This is a really big problem,” Ms. Verdadero said.

Most users do not challenge chatbots when they’ve been given the correct answers, Dr. Bagó said, so the results don’t necessarily mirror widespread behavior in real life. He added that many climate denialists may not even seek information out at all, a phenomenon known as “information avoidance.”

Beyond sycophantic behavior, the team also tested how well chatbots performed on well-established climate facts. They quizzed the 33 models on a battery of 600 questions, including exam and textbook questions about the causes and effects of climate change. The models performed well, averaging above 80 percent for the latest proprietary models like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.

They also tested whether the models performed as well in different languages as they did in English. The team found that accuracy dropped significantly for languages spoken across South Asia and East Africa, including Hindi, Urdu and Swahili, which had the lowest score at 78 percent. They also found that the same question would sometimes yield inconsistent or misleading answers.

“These are communities in very climate-vulnerable areas,” Ms. Verdadero said. “The fact that you could get a much less reliable answer is really quite alarming.”

The team also focused on climate policies. The models were tested on around 650 questions about how different climate policies, including carbon taxes, would affect global temperatures by 2100. The responses were benchmarked against a widely used simulation tool called EN-ROADS, which helps scientists predict how policies may affect future warming.

When the models assessed one policy at a time, their accuracy reached nearly 95 percent among the best-performing models. As soon as they were asked to assess how two or more climate policies would interact, their accuracy was statistically similar to blind guessing.

“What this tells us is, with respect to being able to analyze an interplay of climate policies on performance, they are not there yet,” Ms. Verdadero said.

The largest data centers in the United States are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually, almost as much as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark, according to new research.

The study, published on Monday, delivers the first peer-reviewed estimates of carbon dioxide emissions from the country’s biggest data centers since the start of the artificial intelligence boom. Much of the analysis in the study amounted to detective work, underscoring the secrecy under which A.I. companies have been allowed to operate. — Harry Stevens
